May 3 – Yoimiya
May 4 – Kankōsai |Map = {{Location map|Japan Kyoto|label={{ill|Shidori Shrine|de|Shidori-Schrein|ja|倭文神社|zh|倭文神社}}|position=bottom|width=200|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=15|float=center|caption=}} {{Infobox mapframe|zoom=12|marker=religious-shinto|frame-width=200}} }} '''Shidori Shrine''' (倭文神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|de|Shintō-Schrein|ja|神社|zh|神社}} in the Mikochi (みごち) district of {{ill|Yosano|de|Yosano (Gemeinde)|ja|与謝野町|zh|与謝野町}}, {{ill|Yosa District|de|Yosa-gun|ja|与謝郡|zh|与謝郡}}, {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|de|Präfektur Kyōto|ja|京都府|zh|京都府}}. It is a historic shrine recorded as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|de|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社|zh|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|de|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|ja|延喜式神名帳|zh|延喜式神名帳}} compiled in {{ill|927|de|Jahr 927|ja|927年|zh|927年}} ({{ill|Enchō (Japan)|de|Enchō (Ära)|ja|延長 (日本)|zh|延長 (日本)|lt=延長}} 5).『野田川町誌』野田川町、1969年、570頁。 There are fourteen shrines called “Shidori Shrine” (倭文神社) across Japan that appear in the Engishiki, two of which lie in the Tango region of northern Kyoto Prefecture. This article concerns the one recorded as “Shidori Shrine, Tango Province, Yosa District.”「たんご通信5号」丹後リゾート推進連絡協議会、丹後リゾート総合企画株式会社、1996年、10頁。 Both the shrine itself and its annual festival, the Mikochi Hikiyama Festival, were recognized in April {{ill|2017|de|Jahr 2017|ja|2017年|zh|2017年}} ({{ill|Heisei|de|Heisei-Zeit|ja|平成|zh|平成}} 29) by the {{ill|Agency for Cultural Affairs|de|Kulturbehörde (Japan)|ja|文化庁|zh|文化庁}} as part of the “{{ill|Tango Chirimen Corridor|de|Seidenstraße von Tango|ja|丹後ちりめん回廊|zh|丹後ちりめん回廊}},” a Japanese Heritage story that conveys the region’s historical and cultural appeal.{{Cite web|和書|author=文化庁|authorlink=文化庁|date=|url=https://www.bunka.go.jp/seisaku/bunkazai/nihon_isan/pdf/nihon_isan_pamphlet_2019.pdf|title=日本遺産認定ストーリー一覧|work=「日本遺産（Japan Heritage）」について|accessdate=2020-11-11}}{{Cite web|和書|author=文化庁|authorlink=文化庁|date=|url=https://japan-heritage.bunka.go.jp/ja/stories/story043/index.html|title=300年を紡ぐ絹が織り成す丹後ちりめん回廊|website=日本遺産ポータルサイト|accessdate=2020-11-11}} == History == [[File:倭文神社（京都府与謝野町）.jpg|thumb|Shidori Shrine (Yosa), front view]] According to various records, the shrine was founded in {{ill|710|de|Jahr 710|ja|710年|zh|710年}} ({{ill|Wadō|de|Wadō-Zeit|ja|和銅|zh|和銅}} 3) or {{ill|712|de|Jahr 712|ja|712年|zh|712年}} (Wadō 5), when the deity Shidori no Ōkami was enshrined on Ishizaki Mountain in the village of Osa. At that time, Imperial orders to weave high-quality textiles (called “ayanishiki”A term for fine silk fabric.) were carried out in the area, and it is said that Laughing Oshi from the {{ill|Amabe clan|de|Amabe-Clan|ja|海部氏|zh|海部氏}} at {{ill|Kono Shrine|de|Kono-Schrein|ja|籠神社|zh|籠神社}}, the Ichinomiya of {{ill|Tango Province|de|Tango (Provinz)|ja|丹後国|zh|丹後国}}, was granted an imperial command to enshrine the deity. Legend holds that {{ill|Emperor Daigo|de|Kaiser Daigo|ja|醍醐天皇|zh|醍醐天皇}} also worshiped here.From the explanatory board at the shrine office (社務所). In {{ill|981|de|Jahr 981|ja|981年|zh|981年}} ({{ill|Tenroku|de|Tenroku-Zeit|ja|天禄|zh|天禄}} 12) the shrine was raised to Second Rank, and in {{ill|1223|de|Jahr 1223|ja|1223年|zh|1223年}} ({{ill|Teiō|de|Teiō-Zeit|ja|貞応|zh|貞応}} 2) it was relocated to its current site.{{Cite web|和書|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181009064805/http://www.geocities.jp/engisiki/tango/bun/tag390213-01.html |title=丹後国式内社 |publisher=阜嵐健|accessdate=2018-07-08}} Shrine tradition states that “in ancient times, people gathered under the sacred tree of the deity, offered treasures, made offerings, and rang treasure vessels to pray for a good harvest,” and a bronze bell was later unearthed in the precincts. Since ancient times, local residents of Mikochi have worshiped Shidori Shrine as their {{ill|Ubusuna-gami|de|Ubusuna-Gott|ja|産土神|zh|产土神}}.江原護『古代への旅 丹後』アジェンダ・プロジェクト、2004年、127頁。 Weaving remains a key local industry, best known through {{ill|Tango chirimen|de|Tango-Chirimen|ja|丹後ちりめん|zh|丹後ちりめん}}, and on festival days people from nearby villages traditionally came en masse carrying bundles of hemp fiber.『京都の社寺建築 与謝・丹後編』京都府埋蔵文化財保護基金、1984年、132頁。 An ink inscription from {{ill|1808|de|Jahr 1808|ja|1808年|zh|1808年}} ({{ill|Culture (era)|de|Ära Bunka|ja|文化|zh|文化}} 5) was discovered on the shrine’s roof during repairs. In earlier periods, under {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|de|Shinbutsu-shūgō|ja|神仏習合|zh|神仏習合}}, the shrine was variously known as “Ishizaki Daimyōjin” or “Ishizaki Shidori Daimyōjin.” However, after the early Meiji {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|de|Shinbutsu-bunri|ja|神仏分離令|zh|神仏分離令}} policy separated Shinto and Buddhism, it was officially renamed “Shidori Shrine.” In {{ill|1907|de|Jahr 1907|ja|1907年|zh|1907年}} (Meiji 40), the shrine was designated for {{ill|heihakusai|en}} (imperial offerings). In {{ill|1873|de|Jahr 1873|ja|1873年|zh|1873年}} (Meiji 6) it was ranked as a Village Shrine, and in {{ill|1944|de|Jahr 1944|ja|1944年|zh|1944年}} (Showa 19), on November 20, it was elevated to Prefectural Shrine.神祗院第19第33號 At that time, there were originally two annual festivals—on April 25 and on May 1 when imperial offerings were presented—but nowadays only the spring festival in early May remains.『野田川町誌』野田川町、1969年、411頁。 In {{ill|2017|de|Jahr 2017|ja|2017年|zh|2017年}} (Heisei 29), the shrine and its spring festival, the Mikochi Hikiyama Festival, were officially recognized as part of the Japan Heritage “Tango Chirimen Corridor.”{{Cite web|和書|author=文化庁|authorlink=|date=|url=https://www.bunka.go.jp/seisaku/bunkazai/nihon_isan/|title=「日本遺産（Japan Heritage）」について|work=|language=日本語|accessdate=2018-2-20}}{{Cite web|和書|author=文化庁|authorlink=|date=|url=https://japan-heritage.bunka.go.jp/ja/stories/story043/index.html|title=日本遺産ポータルサイト「丹後ちりめん回廊」|work=|language=日本語|accessdate=2018-2-20}} == Enshrined Deities and Subsidiary Shrines == The main enshrined deity is {{ill|Amano-hatsuchio no Kami|de|Amano-hatsuchio no Kami|ja|天羽槌雄神|1=Takehazuchi|2=ja|3=天羽槌雄神|4=zh|5=天羽槌雄神|6=fr|7=Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi|zh|天羽槌雄神}}, also known as {{ill|Takehazuchi no Mikoto|de|Takehazuchi no Mikoto|ja|建葉槌命|zh|建葉槌命}}. Descendants of the ancient {{ill|Shidori clan|en}} revere him as Shidori no Ōkami. According to mythology, when {{ill|Amaterasu|de|Amaterasu|ja|天照大神|zh|天照大神}} hid in the Heavenly Rock Cave, this god was commanded by {{ill|Takamimusubi|de|Takamimusubi|ja|高皇産霊神|zh|高皇産霊神}} to weave cloth, thus becoming the ancestral deity of weaving. He is also regarded as a god of martial valor, often worshipped together with the war deity {{ill|Hachiman|de|Hachiman|ja|八幡神|zh|八幡神}}.「三河内曳山祭パンフレット」与謝野町三河内区曳山連合会、どでさっさ共和国、2018年 As for subsidiary shrines within the grounds, facing from the large torii on the prefectural road, there is an {{ill|Awashima Shrine|de|Awashima-Schrein|ja|粟嶋神社|zh|粟嶋神社}} on the right, an {{ill|Inari Shrine|de|Inari-Schrein|ja|稲荷神社|zh|稻荷神社}} partway toward the haiden on the right, and a Wakamiya Shrine (若宮社) on the left. File:倭文神社(与謝) 粟嶋社（鳥居右）.jpg|Awashima Shrine File:倭文神社(与謝) 稲荷社（向かって右）.jpg|Inari Shrine File:倭文神社(与謝) 若宮社 (向かって左).jpg|Wakamiya Shrine == Precinct and Cultural Properties == === Buildings === In addition to the main hall, dance stage, and worship hall which stand in a row, the precinct includes a storehouse, shrine gate, administrative office, and so on. The main hall was rebuilt after a fire in the Ka’ei era. According to the shrine’s “Rekidaiki” record, the current structure dates from {{ill|1821|de|Jahr 1821|ja|1821年|zh|1821年}} ({{ill|Bunsei|de|Bunsei-Zeit|ja|文政|zh|文政}} 4). It is an {{ill|irimoya-zukuri|en}} with copper roofing, a typical one-bay design. A karahafu-gabled {{ill|kouhai (architecture)|en|向拝}} extends from the front. The hall has balconies on three sides, with a protruding platform and steps in front. There are carved wooden doors on the front (double-folding) and sides (two-panel), and the interior divides into an inner sanctum and an even deeper sanctuary. The hall’s pillars are secured by beams and clamps, and a notable feature is its complex bracket structure (two-step brackets with additional bracket arms supporting round rafters, plus decorative patterns). The coffered ceiling of the kouhai is typical of Edo-period Tango shrines, also seen at the {{ill|Hiyoshi Shrine (Miyazu)|ja|日吉神社 (宮津市)|zh|日吉神社 (宮津市)}} main hall (built in {{ill|1688|de|Jahr 1688|ja|1688年|zh|1688年}}) and the tutelary shrine at {{ill|Nariai-ji|de|Nariai-ji|ja|成相寺|zh|成相寺}} (built in {{ill|1676|de|Jahr 1676|ja|1676年|zh|1676年}}). The rich carvings on the side panels and doors, including motifs from the Chinese legend of Huang Shigong and Zhang Liang, lions, and peonies, show a resemblance to the famed Karamon gate of the {{ill|Nishi Hongan-ji|de|Nishi Hongan-ji|ja|西本願寺|zh|西本願寺}} in Kyoto. As an important example of late-Edo-era shrine architecture in Tango, it was designated a Kyoto Prefectural Cultural Property in {{ill|1996|de|Jahr 1996|ja|1996年|zh|1996年}} (Heisei 8).{{Cite web|和書|url=http://www.kyoto-be.ne.jp/bunkazai/cms/?page_id=271 |title=京都府指定文化財一覧|publisher=京都府教育庁指導部文化財保護課|accessdate=2018-07-08}} The shinmon (main gate) has a gabled roof with pantiles, is three bays wide, one bay deep, and stands on eight pillars. The haiden (worship hall) is irimoya-zukuri with pantiles, six bays along the front, and a one-bay extension in front. File:倭文神社(与謝).jpg|Midway torii. Inari Shrine (right), Wakamiya Shrine (left). File:倭文神社(与謝) 神門.jpg|Shinmon File:倭文神社（京都府与謝野町）3.jpg|Haiden File:倭文神社(与謝) 拝殿.jpg|Haiden, with the dance stage and main hall behind it. File:倭文神社（京都府与謝野町）4.jpg|View from the dance stage to the main hall File:倭文神社（京都府与謝野町）5.jpg|The main hall File:倭文神社（京都府与謝野町）6.jpg|Main hall exterior File:倭文神社(与謝)本殿（江戸時代後期）.jpg|Main hall ceiling area (front) File:倭文神社(与謝)本殿（江戸時代後期）左側面.jpg|Carvings (left side panel) File:倭文神社(与謝)本殿（江戸時代後期）左.jpg|Ceiling area (left side) File:倭文神社(与謝)本殿（江戸時代後期）右側面.jpg|Carvings (right side panel) File:倭文神社(与謝)本殿（江戸時代後期）右.jpg|Ceiling area (right side) File:倭文神社（京都府与謝野町）7.jpg|Exterior of haiden, dance stage, and main hall === Historic Sites === Within the shrine precincts lie four ancient tumuli known as the Ishizaki Tombs or Shidori Shrine Kofun Group: Mound #1 (circular, 4 m high, 15 m diameter), #2 (circular, 2.5 m high, 10 m diameter), #3 (circular, 2 m high, 7 m diameter), and one keyhole-shaped tumulus about 60 m in total length. Their direct relationship to the shrine is not clearly established, but they are presumed to date to the mid-Kofun period (5th century). A Preservation Society was formed in {{ill|1930|de|Jahr 1930|ja|1930年|zh|1930年}} (Showa 5). From the tumuli, there is a panoramic view of Mikochi district and Mount Ōe. The entire shrine area is protected as part of the “Shidori Shrine Cultural Properties Preservation District” by Kyoto Prefecture.{{Cite web|和書|url=http://www.pref.kyoto.jp/kankyo/rdb/eco/sd/sd027.html |title=文化財環境保全地区 |publisher=京都府|accessdate=2018-07-08}} File:倭文神社（京都府与謝野町）２.jpg|Precinct view File:倭文神社(与謝) 古墳群.jpg|Four ancient tombs on the left side of the grounds File:倭文神社(与謝)古墳群上から.jpg|Looking down toward the shrine from the tombs File:倭文神社(与謝)古墳群からの眺望.jpg|Panorama from the tumuli == External Subsidiary Shrines == In addition to the main precinct, the shrine maintains outer shrines scattered around the town: Takamine-sha on Okadayama, Ozaki Kojinsha in Umedani, Atago-sha in Okuyama, Ebisu-sha in Daidō, Itsukushima-sha in Moriya, Shibunashi-sha in Nakatsubo, and Osaoka-sha further in the interior.『野田川町誌』野田川町、1969年、571頁。 There is also an Inari-sha in Fukumori. == Parishioners and the Mikochi Hikiyama Festival == [[File:三河内曳山祭４.jpg|thumb|Mikochi Hikiyama Festival procession]] [[File:三河内曳山祭2.jpg|thumb|The procession enters Miyamae Street]] [[File:倭文神社(与謝)参道.jpg|thumb|Miyamae Street]] This annual festival is said to have started in {{ill|1755|de|Jahr 1755|ja|1755年|zh|1755年}} ({{ill|Hōreki|de|Hōreki-Zeit|ja|宝暦|zh|宝暦}} 5) and flourished with the growth of the local textile industry, {{ill|Tango chirimen|de|Tango-Chirimen|ja|丹後ちりめん|zh|丹後ちりめん}}. It was once called the Hassaku Festival, held on the first day of the eighth month of the lunar calendar, but around {{ill|1887|de|Jahr 1887|ja|1887年|zh|1887年}} (Meiji 20) it became part of the {{ill|Kayadani Festival|en}} for the nearby {{ill|Tenman Shrine (Kayacho)|en|天満神社 (加悦)|ja|天満神社 (京都府与謝野町)|zh|天満神社 (京都府与謝野町)}} and took place every April 24–25. In {{ill|1991|de|Jahr 1991|ja|1991年|zh|1991年}} (Heisei 3), it separated from the Kayadani Festival and was moved to May 3–4.Because weaving declined and more parishioners took jobs requiring weekday attendance, they could no longer assemble the heavy floats on weekdays.京都新聞社『ふるさとNEXT 京都府北部地域で生きる』京都新聞出版センター、2018年、164-165頁。 This event, officially called the “Mikochi Hikiyama Gyōji,” is designated a Kyoto Prefecture {{ill|Intangible Folk Cultural Property|de|immaterielles Volkskulturgut|ja|無形民俗文化財|zh|无形民俗文化财}}.{{Cite web|和書|url=http://www.kyoto-kankou.or.jp/info_search/?event_id=7548&r=1531059533.3514 |title=三河内曳山祭 |publisher=|accessdate=2018-07-08}} '''The Mikochi Hikiyama Festival''' begins May 2 with the Shinkōsai, continues May 3 with a vigil (Yoimiya), and culminates on May 4 with the main festival day including sacred dances, the “calling of the gods” (kamiobiki), float processions, and the Kankōsai that returns the deities to their seats. === Float Procession (Hikiyama) === A giant banner leads the parade, followed by Kaguraden, large mountain floats, smaller children’s floats, and so on—about twelve floats in total. The largest are the yama (mountain) floats and the gei (performance) floats, which alternate participation every other year. In {{ill|2018|de|Jahr 2018|ja|2018年|zh|2018年}} (Heisei 30), the yama floats made the rounds. Parishioners from six sub-districts of Mikochi gather at their boundary lines with matching happi coats, bringing their floats. The giant banner from Umeya leads, followed by shrine officials, men carrying halberds and umbrellas, then each district’s floats.『野田川町誌』野田川町、1969年、412-413頁。 From the community center, one can see the line of floats in a long procession. Each yama float has its own musical accompaniment, while the children’s taiko float beats a large drum. Upon reaching the great torii and entering Miyamae Street, all converge on the same rhythm, called Tenjin-bayashi, with shouts of “dodesassa, dodesassa” and the pounding drum “dodendon-don, dodendon-don.”江原護『古代への旅 丹後』アジェンダ・プロジェクト、2004年、128頁。 During the procession, the “kamiobiki” (god-invitation) rite takes place, and once arrived at Shidori Shrine, ceremonial dances are offered. In the past, the kagura dancers would also make rounds to purify each home’s hearth, but now that survives only in an abbreviated form at the eve of the festival (May 3) in front of the shrine and each float, as well as in brief offerings on the morning of May 4. Below is a general table of the main floats and their characteristics. {| class="wikitable" |+Key floats of the Mikochi Hikiyama Festival !Parish (District)!!Float Name!!Enshrined Kami!!Crest!!Happi Coat!!Music/Chant Variety!!Float Notes |- |Umeya (Ōnobori) |Ōnobori Banner |{{ill|Amano-hatsuchio no Kami|de|Amano-hatsuchio no Kami|ja|天羽槌雄神|1=Takehazuchi|2=ja|3=天羽槌雄神|4=zh|5=天羽槌雄神|6=fr|7=Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi|zh|天羽槌雄神}} |Maru-ni-mitsu-aoi (triple hollyhock) |Crest on back; “Ōnobori” on collar; eight plum blossoms at hem |N/A |~6m high, 1.6m wide, 3.3m deep |- |Nakagumi |Hachiman-yama |{{ill|Emperor Ōjin|de|Kaiser Ōjin|ja|応神天皇|zh|应神天皇}} (Honada Wake no Mikoto) |Clustered arrows |Doves throughout the design |Various chants: “Yāma yāma,” “Kōrya kōrya,” “Tentetsu-shan-shan,” “Hotei-bayashi,” “Ichichiri hyu-hyuttose,” “Hanagasa-ondo,” “Oppiki taitaino-e,” “Beppin naika,” “O-mawari,” “hayashi-komi,” etc. |Height ~4.6m, width ~2.95m, depth ~3.62m |- |Shidori-chō |Shidori-yama |Shidori no Ōkami |Maru-ni-mitsu-aoi |Hollyhock leaves plus an itoguruma (thread-spinning wheel), symbol of weaving |Various: “Hayashi-komi,” “Yāma yāma,” “Kōrya kōrya,” “Doshitai doshitai,” “Ikkyō āiya,” “Manda,” “Tenjin-bayashi,” “Hādondon,” “Ākorya-korya,” “Beppin naika,” “Kompira fune fune,” “Hitotsutosei,” “Oppiki taitai,” etc. |Height ~4.7m, width ~3m, depth ~3.65m |- |Omotemachi |Kasuga-yama |{{ill|Takemikazuchi|de|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌神|zh|武甕槌神}} (Kashima no Ōkami) |Descending wisteria |Falling maple leaves and flowing water pattern |Tenjin-bayashi, Ikken-sho, Juuni-kagura, Koma, Hotei-bayashi, Take-bayashi, Mawari, “Kompira fune fune,” “Oppiki taitai,” “Kazuu-ta,” etc. (many) |Began with a carried float in {{ill|Culture 3|en}}, turned into a yama float in Meiji 25. Height ~4.5m, width 3m, depth 3.7m. Formerly limited to male performers, but from {{ill|2016|de|Jahr 2016|ja|2016年|zh|2016年}} (Heisei 28) females also participate on the float. |- |Kaminomachi |Urashima-yama |{{ill|Kagutsuchi|de|Kagutsuchi|ja|カグツチ|zh|迦具土}} (Atago deity) and {{ill|Ukemochi no Kami|en}} (Inari deity) |Single turtle in a circle |Crest of waves |Many: Tenjin-bayashi, Ikken-sho, Koma, Juuni-kagura, Sasa-bayashi, Hotei-bayashi, “Take ni suzume,” “Yuka-shita,” “O-mawari,” etc. |Formed in Meiji 25 when the towns worshipping Atago and Inari merged. Height ~4.87m, width 3.31m, depth 4.24m. |- |Kagura-chō |Kagura-den |Shishi-gashira (lion’s head) |Mitsu-domoe |Three commas plus peonies |Gion-bayashi. Dances include hei-no-mai, ken-no-mai, shihō-kake, midare-no-mai, etc. |~3.65m tall, 2.27m wide, 3.15m deep |} === Kamiobiki (“Calling the Gods”) === Also called “kamiobi” in local speech. According to oral tradition, the shrine’s main deity, {{ill|Amano-hatsuchio no Kami|de|Amano-hatsuchio no Kami|ja|天羽槌雄神|1=Takehazuchi|2=ja|3=天羽槌雄神|4=zh|5=天羽槌雄神|6=fr|7=Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi|zh|天羽槌雄神}}, was once married to {{ill|Suseri-hime|de|Suseri-Hime|ja|須勢理媛|zh|須勢理媛}}, enshrined at {{ill|Sushiro Shrine|en|須代神社|ja|須代神社|zh|須代神社}} in the nearby Akashi district across the river. However, because Suseri-hime became the principal wife of the mighty {{ill|Ōkuninushi|de|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主命|zh|大国主命}}, the two were forced to part ways, and they can reunite only during this annual festival. During the float procession, at the Sugikoshi Bridge over the Okuyama River, participants pour sacred sake and rice into the river three times. A representative from Umeya holds up a gohei and calls eastward with three loud “Ō~i!” In local lore, Suseri-hime rests beneath the “pine tree on the riverbank” at the halfway point of the {{ill|Nodagawa (Kyoto)|de|Nodagawa (Fluss)|ja|野田川 (京都府)|zh|野田川}}, hears the call, and joins the procession so she and her husband can be together again for the festival. It is also said that her brothers, {{ill|Kuraokami no Kami|en}} (the deity of rice) and {{ill|Ame no mikumari no Kami|en}} (the deity of offering), join in at the same call, thus forming a group of deities who jointly conduct the festival. == Access == ;Address * 1453 Mikochi, {{ill|Yosano|de|Yosano (Gemeinde)|ja|与謝野町|zh|与謝野町}}, {{ill|Yosa District|de|Yosa-gun|ja|与謝郡|zh|与謝郡}}, {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|de|Präfektur Kyōto|ja|京都府|zh|京都府}} ;Transportation * From {{ill|Yosano Station|en|与謝野駅|ja|与謝野駅|zh|与謝野駅}} on the {{ill|Kyoto Tango Railway|de|Kyoto Tango Bahn|ja|京都丹後鉄道|zh|京都丹後鉄道}}, take a bus by {{ill|Kaya Kōsan|en}} and get off at “Mikochi-guchi.”江原護『古代への旅 丹後』アジェンダ・プロジェクト、2004年、129頁。 * Take the {{ill|Tankai Bus|en|丹海バス|ja|丹海バス|zh|丹海バス}} Yosa or Fukuchiyama lines to “Mikochi Elementary School Stop.” == Notes == == References == == Further Reading == * 江原護『古代への旅 丹後』アジェンダ・プロジェクト、2004年 * 『野田川町誌』野田川町、1969年 * 『京都の社寺建築 与謝・丹後編』京都府埋蔵文化財保護基金、1984年 * 「三河内曳山祭パンフレット」与謝野町三河内区曳山連合会、どでさっさ共和国、2018年 In {{ill|1996|de|Jahr 1996|ja|1996年|zh|1996年}} ({{ill|Heisei|de|Heisei-Zeit|ja|平成|zh|平成}} 8) designated as a Kyoto Prefectural Cultural Property. |Alternative name = Ishizaki Shidori Daimyōjin |Fuda places etc.= |Annual festival= May 4 – Mikochi Hikiyama Festival (registered as Kyoto Prefecture Intangible Folk Cultural Property) |Shinto rituals = May 2 – Shinkōsai
May 3 – Yoimiya
May 4 – Kankōsai |Map = {{Location map|Japan Kyoto|label={{ill|Shidori Shrine|de|Shidori-Schrein|ja|倭文神社|zh|倭文神社}}|position=bottom|width=200|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=15|float=center|caption=}} {{Infobox mapframe|zoom=12|marker=religious-shinto|frame-width=200}} }} '''Shidori Shrine''' (倭文神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|de|Shintō-Schrein|ja|神社|zh|神社}} in the Mikochi (みごち) district of {{ill|Yosano|de|Yosano (Gemeinde)|ja|与謝野町|zh|与謝野町}}, {{ill|Yosa District|de|Yosa-gun|ja|与謝郡|zh|与謝郡}}, {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|de|Präfektur Kyōto|ja|京都府|zh|京都府}}. It is a historic shrine recorded as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|de|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社|zh|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|de|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|ja|延喜式神名帳|zh|延喜式神名帳}} compiled in {{ill|927|de|Jahr 927|ja|927年|zh|927年}} ({{ill|Enchō (Japan)|de|Enchō (Ära)|ja|延長 (日本)|zh|延長 (日本)|lt=延長}} 5).『野田川町誌』野田川町、1969年、570頁。 There are fourteen shrines called “Shidori Shrine” (倭文神社) across Japan that appear in the Engishiki, two of which lie in the Tango region of northern Kyoto Prefecture. This article concerns the one recorded as “Shidori Shrine, Tango Province, Yosa District.”「たんご通信5号」丹後リゾート推進連絡協議会、丹後リゾート総合企画株式会社、1996年、10頁。 Both the shrine itself and its annual festival, the Mikochi Hikiyama Festival, were recognized in April {{ill|2017|de|Jahr 2017|ja|2017年|zh|2017年}} ({{ill|Heisei|de|Heisei-Zeit|ja|平成|zh|平成}} 29) by the {{ill|Agency for Cultural Affairs|de|Kulturbehörde (Japan)|ja|文化庁|zh|文化庁}} as part of the “{{ill|Tango Chirimen Corridor|de|Seidenstraße von Tango|ja|丹後ちりめん回廊|zh|丹後ちりめん回廊}},” a Japanese Heritage story that conveys the region’s historical and cultural appeal.{{Cite web|和書|author=文化庁|authorlink=文化庁|date=|url=https://www.bunka.go.jp/seisaku/bunkazai/nihon_isan/pdf/nihon_isan_pamphlet_2019.pdf|title=日本遺産認定ストーリー一覧|work=「日本遺産（Japan Heritage）」について|accessdate=2020-11-11}}{{Cite web|和書|author=文化庁|authorlink=文化庁|date=|url=https://japan-heritage.bunka.go.jp/ja/stories/story043/index.html|title=300年を紡ぐ絹が織り成す丹後ちりめん回廊|website=日本遺産ポータルサイト|accessdate=2020-11-11}} == History == [[File:倭文神社（京都府与謝野町）.jpg|thumb|Shidori Shrine (Yosa), front view]] According to various records, the shrine was founded in {{ill|710|de|Jahr 710|ja|710年|zh|710年}} ({{ill|Wadō|de|Wadō-Zeit|ja|和銅|zh|和銅}} 3) or {{ill|712|de|Jahr 712|ja|712年|zh|712年}} (Wadō 5), when the deity Shidori no Ōkami was enshrined on Ishizaki Mountain in the village of Osa. At that time, Imperial orders to weave high-quality textiles (called “ayanishiki”A term for fine silk fabric.) were carried out in the area, and it is said that Laughing Oshi from the {{ill|Amabe clan|de|Amabe-Clan|ja|海部氏|zh|海部氏}} at {{ill|Kono Shrine|de|Kono-Schrein|ja|籠神社|zh|籠神社}}, the Ichinomiya of {{ill|Tango Province|de|Tango (Provinz)|ja|丹後国|zh|丹後国}}, was granted an imperial command to enshrine the deity. Legend holds that {{ill|Emperor Daigo|de|Kaiser Daigo|ja|醍醐天皇|zh|醍醐天皇}} also worshiped here.From the explanatory board at the shrine office (社務所). In {{ill|981|de|Jahr 981|ja|981年|zh|981年}} ({{ill|Tenroku|de|Tenroku-Zeit|ja|天禄|zh|天禄}} 12) the shrine was raised to Second Rank, and in {{ill|1223|de|Jahr 1223|ja|1223年|zh|1223年}} ({{ill|Teiō|de|Teiō-Zeit|ja|貞応|zh|貞応}} 2) it was relocated to its current site.{{Cite web|和書|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181009064805/http://www.geocities.jp/engisiki/tango/bun/tag390213-01.html |title=丹後国式内社 |publisher=阜嵐健|accessdate=2018-07-08}} Shrine tradition states that “in ancient times, people gathered under the sacred tree of the deity, offered treasures, made offerings, and rang treasure vessels to pray for a good harvest,” and a bronze bell was later unearthed in the precincts. Since ancient times, local residents of Mikochi have worshiped Shidori Shrine as their {{ill|Ubusuna-gami|de|Ubusuna-Gott|ja|産土神|zh|产土神}}.江原護『古代への旅 丹後』アジェンダ・プロジェクト、2004年、127頁。 Weaving remains a key local industry, best known through {{ill|Tango chirimen|de|Tango-Chirimen|ja|丹後ちりめん|zh|丹後ちりめん}}, and on festival days people from nearby villages traditionally came en masse carrying bundles of hemp fiber.『京都の社寺建築 与謝・丹後編』京都府埋蔵文化財保護基金、1984年、132頁。 An ink inscription from {{ill|1808|de|Jahr 1808|ja|1808年|zh|1808年}} ({{ill|Culture (era)|de|Ära Bunka|ja|文化|1=Bunka|2=ja|3=文化 (元号)|4=de|5=Bunka (Ära)|6=ko|7=분카|zh|文化}} 5) was discovered on the shrine’s roof during repairs. In earlier periods, under {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|de|Shinbutsu-shūgō|ja|神仏習合|zh|神仏習合}}, the shrine was variously known as “Ishizaki Daimyōjin” or “Ishizaki Shidori Daimyōjin.” However, after the early Meiji {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|de|Shinbutsu-bunri|ja|神仏分離令|zh|神仏分離令}} policy separated Shinto and Buddhism, it was officially renamed “Shidori Shrine.” In {{ill|1907|de|Jahr 1907|ja|1907年|zh|1907年}} (Meiji 40), the shrine was designated for {{ill|heihakusai|en}} (imperial offerings). In {{ill|1873|de|Jahr 1873|ja|1873年|zh|1873年}} (Meiji 6) it was ranked as a Village Shrine, and in {{ill|1944|de|Jahr 1944|ja|1944年|zh|1944年}} (Showa 19), on November 20, it was elevated to Prefectural Shrine.神祗院第19第33號 At that time, there were originally two annual festivals—on April 25 and on May 1 when imperial offerings were presented—but nowadays only the spring festival in early May remains.『野田川町誌』野田川町、1969年、411頁。 In {{ill|2017|de|Jahr 2017|ja|2017年|zh|2017年}} (Heisei 29), the shrine and its spring festival, the Mikochi Hikiyama Festival, were officially recognized as part of the Japan Heritage “Tango Chirimen Corridor.”{{Cite web|和書|author=文化庁|authorlink=|date=|url=https://www.bunka.go.jp/seisaku/bunkazai/nihon_isan/|title=「日本遺産（Japan Heritage）」について|work=|language=日本語|accessdate=2018-2-20}}{{Cite web|和書|author=文化庁|authorlink=|date=|url=https://japan-heritage.bunka.go.jp/ja/stories/story043/index.html|title=日本遺産ポータルサイト「丹後ちりめん回廊」|work=|language=日本語|accessdate=2018-2-20}} == Enshrined Deities and Subsidiary Shrines == The main enshrined deity is {{ill|Amano-hatsuchio no Kami|de|Amano-hatsuchio no Kami|ja|天羽槌雄神|1=Takehazuchi|2=ja|3=天羽槌雄神|4=zh|5=天羽槌雄神|6=fr|7=Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi|zh|天羽槌雄神}}, also known as {{ill|Takehazuchi no Mikoto|de|Takehazuchi no Mikoto|ja|建葉槌命|zh|建葉槌命}}. Descendants of the ancient {{ill|Shidori clan|en}} revere him as Shidori no Ōkami. According to mythology, when {{ill|Amaterasu|de|Amaterasu|ja|天照大神|zh|天照大神}} hid in the Heavenly Rock Cave, this god was commanded by {{ill|Takamimusubi|de|Takamimusubi|ja|高皇産霊神|zh|高皇産霊神}} to weave cloth, thus becoming the ancestral deity of weaving. He is also regarded as a god of martial valor, often worshipped together with the war deity {{ill|Hachiman|de|Hachiman|ja|八幡神|zh|八幡神}}.「三河内曳山祭パンフレット」与謝野町三河内区曳山連合会、どでさっさ共和国、2018年 As for subsidiary shrines within the grounds, facing from the large torii on the prefectural road, there is an {{ill|Awashima Shrine|de|Awashima-Schrein|ja|粟嶋神社|zh|粟嶋神社}} on the right, an {{ill|Inari Shrine|de|Inari-Schrein|ja|稲荷神社|zh|稻荷神社}} partway toward the haiden on the right, and a Wakamiya Shrine (若宮社) on the left. File:倭文神社(与謝) 粟嶋社（鳥居右）.jpg|Awashima Shrine File:倭文神社(与謝) 稲荷社（向かって右）.jpg|Inari Shrine File:倭文神社(与謝) 若宮社 (向かって左).jpg|Wakamiya Shrine == Precinct and Cultural Properties == === Buildings === In addition to the main hall, dance stage, and worship hall which stand in a row, the precinct includes a storehouse, shrine gate, administrative office, and so on. The main hall was rebuilt after a fire in the Ka’ei era. According to the shrine’s “Rekidaiki” record, the current structure dates from {{ill|1821|de|Jahr 1821|ja|1821年|zh|1821年}} ({{ill|Bunsei|de|Bunsei-Zeit|ja|文政|zh|文政}} 4). It is an {{ill|irimoya-zukuri|en}} with copper roofing, a typical one-bay design. A karahafu-gabled {{ill|kouhai (architecture)|en|向拝}} extends from the front. The hall has balconies on three sides, with a protruding platform and steps in front. There are carved wooden doors on the front (double-folding) and sides (two-panel), and the interior divides into an inner sanctum and an even deeper sanctuary. The hall’s pillars are secured by beams and clamps, and a notable feature is its complex bracket structure (two-step brackets with additional bracket arms supporting round rafters, plus decorative patterns). The coffered ceiling of the kouhai is typical of Edo-period Tango shrines, also seen at the {{ill|Hiyoshi Shrine (Miyazu)|ja|日吉神社 (宮津市)|zh|日吉神社 (宮津市)}} main hall (built in {{ill|1688|de|Jahr 1688|ja|1688年|zh|1688年}}) and the tutelary shrine at {{ill|Nariai-ji|de|Nariai-ji|ja|成相寺|zh|成相寺}} (built in {{ill|1676|de|Jahr 1676|ja|1676年|zh|1676年}}). The rich carvings on the side panels and doors, including motifs from the Chinese legend of Huang Shigong and Zhang Liang, lions, and peonies, show a resemblance to the famed Karamon gate of the {{ill|Nishi Hongan-ji|de|Nishi Hongan-ji|ja|西本願寺|zh|西本願寺}} in Kyoto. As an important example of late-Edo-era shrine architecture in Tango, it was designated a Kyoto Prefectural Cultural Property in {{ill|1996|de|Jahr 1996|ja|1996年|zh|1996年}} (Heisei 8).{{Cite web|和書|url=http://www.kyoto-be.ne.jp/bunkazai/cms/?page_id=271 |title=京都府指定文化財一覧|publisher=京都府教育庁指導部文化財保護課|accessdate=2018-07-08}} The shinmon (main gate) has a gabled roof with pantiles, is three bays wide, one bay deep, and stands on eight pillars. The haiden (worship hall) is irimoya-zukuri with pantiles, six bays along the front, and a one-bay extension in front. File:倭文神社(与謝).jpg|Midway torii. Inari Shrine (right), Wakamiya Shrine (left). File:倭文神社(与謝) 神門.jpg|Shinmon File:倭文神社（京都府与謝野町）3.jpg|Haiden File:倭文神社(与謝) 拝殿.jpg|Haiden, with the dance stage and main hall behind it. File:倭文神社（京都府与謝野町）4.jpg|View from the dance stage to the main hall File:倭文神社（京都府与謝野町）5.jpg|The main hall File:倭文神社（京都府与謝野町）6.jpg|Main hall exterior File:倭文神社(与謝)本殿（江戸時代後期）.jpg|Main hall ceiling area (front) File:倭文神社(与謝)本殿（江戸時代後期）左側面.jpg|Carvings (left side panel) File:倭文神社(与謝)本殿（江戸時代後期）左.jpg|Ceiling area (left side) File:倭文神社(与謝)本殿（江戸時代後期）右側面.jpg|Carvings (right side panel) File:倭文神社(与謝)本殿（江戸時代後期）右.jpg|Ceiling area (right side) File:倭文神社（京都府与謝野町）7.jpg|Exterior of haiden, dance stage, and main hall === Historic Sites === Within the shrine precincts lie four ancient tumuli known as the Ishizaki Tombs or Shidori Shrine Kofun Group: Mound #1 (circular, 4 m high, 15 m diameter), #2 (circular, 2.5 m high, 10 m diameter), #3 (circular, 2 m high, 7 m diameter), and one keyhole-shaped tumulus about 60 m in total length. Their direct relationship to the shrine is not clearly established, but they are presumed to date to the mid-Kofun period (5th century). A Preservation Society was formed in {{ill|1930|de|Jahr 1930|ja|1930年|zh|1930年}} (Showa 5). From the tumuli, there is a panoramic view of Mikochi district and Mount Ōe. The entire shrine area is protected as part of the “Shidori Shrine Cultural Properties Preservation District” by Kyoto Prefecture.{{Cite web|和書|url=http://www.pref.kyoto.jp/kankyo/rdb/eco/sd/sd027.html |title=文化財環境保全地区 |publisher=京都府|accessdate=2018-07-08}} File:倭文神社（京都府与謝野町）２.jpg|Precinct view File:倭文神社(与謝) 古墳群.jpg|Four ancient tombs on the left side of the grounds File:倭文神社(与謝)古墳群上から.jpg|Looking down toward the shrine from the tombs File:倭文神社(与謝)古墳群からの眺望.jpg|Panorama from the tumuli == External Subsidiary Shrines == In addition to the main precinct, the shrine maintains outer shrines scattered around the town: Takamine-sha on Okadayama, Ozaki Kojinsha in Umedani, Atago-sha in Okuyama, Ebisu-sha in Daidō, Itsukushima-sha in Moriya, Shibunashi-sha in Nakatsubo, and Osaoka-sha further in the interior.『野田川町誌』野田川町、1969年、571頁。 There is also an Inari-sha in Fukumori. == Parishioners and the Mikochi Hikiyama Festival == [[File:三河内曳山祭４.jpg|thumb|Mikochi Hikiyama Festival procession]] [[File:三河内曳山祭2.jpg|thumb|The procession enters Miyamae Street]] [[File:倭文神社(与謝)参道.jpg|thumb|Miyamae Street]] This annual festival is said to have started in {{ill|1755|de|Jahr 1755|ja|1755年|zh|1755年}} ({{ill|Hōreki|de|Hōreki-Zeit|ja|宝暦|zh|宝暦}} 5) and flourished with the growth of the local textile industry, {{ill|Tango chirimen|de|Tango-Chirimen|ja|丹後ちりめん|zh|丹後ちりめん}}. It was once called the Hassaku Festival, held on the first day of the eighth month of the lunar calendar, but around {{ill|1887|de|Jahr 1887|ja|1887年|zh|1887年}} (Meiji 20) it became part of the {{ill|Kayadani Festival|en}} for the nearby {{ill|Tenman Shrine (Kayacho)|en|天満神社 (加悦)|ja|天満神社 (京都府与謝野町)|zh|天満神社 (京都府与謝野町)}} and took place every April 24–25. In {{ill|1991|de|Jahr 1991|ja|1991年|zh|1991年}} (Heisei 3), it separated from the Kayadani Festival and was moved to May 3–4.Because weaving declined and more parishioners took jobs requiring weekday attendance, they could no longer assemble the heavy floats on weekdays.京都新聞社『ふるさとNEXT 京都府北部地域で生きる』京都新聞出版センター、2018年、164-165頁。 This event, officially called the “Mikochi Hikiyama Gyōji,” is designated a Kyoto Prefecture {{ill|Intangible Folk Cultural Property|de|immaterielles Volkskulturgut|ja|無形民俗文化財|zh|无形民俗文化财}}.{{Cite web|和書|url=http://www.kyoto-kankou.or.jp/info_search/?event_id=7548&r=1531059533.3514 |title=三河内曳山祭 |publisher=|accessdate=2018-07-08}} '''The Mikochi Hikiyama Festival''' begins May 2 with the Shinkōsai, continues May 3 with a vigil (Yoimiya), and culminates on May 4 with the main festival day including sacred dances, the “calling of the gods” (kamiobiki), float processions, and the Kankōsai that returns the deities to their seats. === Float Procession (Hikiyama) === A giant banner leads the parade, followed by Kaguraden, large mountain floats, smaller children’s floats, and so on—about twelve floats in total. The largest are the yama (mountain) floats and the gei (performance) floats, which alternate participation every other year. In {{ill|2018|de|Jahr 2018|ja|2018年|zh|2018年}} (Heisei 30), the yama floats made the rounds. Parishioners from six sub-districts of Mikochi gather at their boundary lines with matching happi coats, bringing their floats. The giant banner from Umeya leads, followed by shrine officials, men carrying halberds and umbrellas, then each district’s floats.『野田川町誌』野田川町、1969年、412-413頁。 From the community center, one can see the line of floats in a long procession. Each yama float has its own musical accompaniment, while the children’s taiko float beats a large drum. Upon reaching the great torii and entering Miyamae Street, all converge on the same rhythm, called Tenjin-bayashi, with shouts of “dodesassa, dodesassa” and the pounding drum “dodendon-don, dodendon-don.”江原護『古代への旅 丹後』アジェンダ・プロジェクト、2004年、128頁。 During the procession, the “kamiobiki” (god-invitation) rite takes place, and once arrived at Shidori Shrine, ceremonial dances are offered. In the past, the kagura dancers would also make rounds to purify each home’s hearth, but now that survives only in an abbreviated form at the eve of the festival (May 3) in front of the shrine and each float, as well as in brief offerings on the morning of May 4. Below is a general table of the main floats and their characteristics. {| class="wikitable" |+Key floats of the Mikochi Hikiyama Festival !Parish (District)!!Float Name!!Enshrined Kami!!Crest!!Happi Coat!!Music/Chant Variety!!Float Notes |- |Umeya (Ōnobori) |Ōnobori Banner |{{ill|Amano-hatsuchio no Kami|de|Amano-hatsuchio no Kami|ja|天羽槌雄神|1=Takehazuchi|2=ja|3=天羽槌雄神|4=zh|5=天羽槌雄神|6=fr|7=Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi|zh|天羽槌雄神}} |Maru-ni-mitsu-aoi (triple hollyhock) |Crest on back; “Ōnobori” on collar; eight plum blossoms at hem |N/A |~6m high, 1.6m wide, 3.3m deep |- |Nakagumi |Hachiman-yama |{{ill|Emperor Ōjin|de|Kaiser Ōjin|ja|応神天皇|zh|应神天皇}} (Honada Wake no Mikoto) |Clustered arrows |Doves throughout the design |Various chants: “Yāma yāma,” “Kōrya kōrya,” “Tentetsu-shan-shan,” “Hotei-bayashi,” “Ichichiri hyu-hyuttose,” “Hanagasa-ondo,” “Oppiki taitaino-e,” “Beppin naika,” “O-mawari,” “hayashi-komi,” etc. |Height ~4.6m, width ~2.95m, depth ~3.62m |- |Shidori-chō |Shidori-yama |Shidori no Ōkami |Maru-ni-mitsu-aoi |Hollyhock leaves plus an itoguruma (thread-spinning wheel), symbol of weaving |Various: “Hayashi-komi,” “Yāma yāma,” “Kōrya kōrya,” “Doshitai doshitai,” “Ikkyō āiya,” “Manda,” “Tenjin-bayashi,” “Hādondon,” “Ākorya-korya,” “Beppin naika,” “Kompira fune fune,” “Hitotsutosei,” “Oppiki taitai,” etc. |Height ~4.7m, width ~3m, depth ~3.65m |- |Omotemachi |Kasuga-yama |{{ill|Takemikazuchi|de|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌神|zh|武甕槌神}} (Kashima no Ōkami) |Descending wisteria |Falling maple leaves and flowing water pattern |Tenjin-bayashi, Ikken-sho, Juuni-kagura, Koma, Hotei-bayashi, Take-bayashi, Mawari, “Kompira fune fune,” “Oppiki taitai,” “Kazuu-ta,” etc. (many) |Began with a carried float in {{ill|Culture 3|en}}, turned into a yama float in Meiji 25. Height ~4.5m, width 3m, depth 3.7m. Formerly limited to male performers, but from {{ill|2016|de|Jahr 2016|ja|2016年|zh|2016年}} (Heisei 28) females also participate on the float. |- |Kaminomachi |Urashima-yama |{{ill|Kagutsuchi|de|Kagutsuchi|ja|カグツチ|zh|迦具土}} (Atago deity) and {{ill|Ukemochi no Kami|en}} (Inari deity) |Single turtle in a circle |Crest of waves |Many: Tenjin-bayashi, Ikken-sho, Koma, Juuni-kagura, Sasa-bayashi, Hotei-bayashi, “Take ni suzume,” “Yuka-shita,” “O-mawari,” etc. |Formed in Meiji 25 when the towns worshipping Atago and Inari merged. Height ~4.87m, width 3.31m, depth 4.24m. |- |Kagura-chō |Kagura-den |Shishi-gashira (lion’s head) |Mitsu-domoe |Three commas plus peonies |Gion-bayashi. Dances include hei-no-mai, ken-no-mai, shihō-kake, midare-no-mai, etc. |~3.65m tall, 2.27m wide, 3.15m deep |} === Kamiobiki (“Calling the Gods”) === Also called “kamiobi” in local speech. According to oral tradition, the shrine’s main deity, {{ill|Amano-hatsuchio no Kami|de|Amano-hatsuchio no Kami|ja|天羽槌雄神|1=Takehazuchi|2=ja|3=天羽槌雄神|4=zh|5=天羽槌雄神|6=fr|7=Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi|zh|天羽槌雄神}}, was once married to {{ill|Suseri-hime|de|Suseri-Hime|ja|須勢理媛|zh|須勢理媛}}, enshrined at {{ill|Sushiro Shrine|en|須代神社|ja|須代神社|zh|須代神社}} in the nearby Akashi district across the river. However, because Suseri-hime became the principal wife of the mighty {{ill|Ōkuninushi|de|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主命|zh|大国主命}}, the two were forced to part ways, and they can reunite only during this annual festival. During the float procession, at the Sugikoshi Bridge over the Okuyama River, participants pour sacred sake and rice into the river three times. A representative from Umeya holds up a gohei and calls eastward with three loud “Ō~i!” In local lore, Suseri-hime rests beneath the “pine tree on the riverbank” at the halfway point of the {{ill|Nodagawa (Kyoto)|de|Nodagawa (Fluss)|ja|野田川 (京都府)|zh|野田川}}, hears the call, and joins the procession so she and her husband can be together again for the festival. It is also said that her brothers, {{ill|Kuraokami no Kami|en}} (the deity of rice) and {{ill|Ame no mikumari no Kami|en}} (the deity of offering), join in at the same call, thus forming a group of deities who jointly conduct the festival. == Access == ;Address * 1453 Mikochi, {{ill|Yosano|de|Yosano (Gemeinde)|ja|与謝野町|zh|与謝野町}}, {{ill|Yosa District|de|Yosa-gun|ja|与謝郡|zh|与謝郡}}, {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|de|Präfektur Kyōto|ja|京都府|zh|京都府}} ;Transportation * From {{ill|Yosano Station|en|与謝野駅|ja|与謝野駅|zh|与謝野駅}} on the {{ill|Kyoto Tango Railway|de|Kyoto Tango Bahn|ja|京都丹後鉄道|zh|京都丹後鉄道}}, take a bus by {{ill|Kaya Kōsan|en}} and get off at “Mikochi-guchi.”江原護『古代への旅 丹後』アジェンダ・プロジェクト、2004年、129頁。 * Take the {{ill|Tankai Bus|en|丹海バス|ja|丹海バス|zh|丹海バス}} Yosa or Fukuchiyama lines to “Mikochi Elementary School Stop.” == Notes == == References == == Further Reading == * 江原護『古代への旅 丹後』アジェンダ・プロジェクト、2004年 * 『野田川町誌』野田川町、1969年 * 『京都の社寺建築 与謝・丹後編』京都府埋蔵文化財保護基金、1984年 * 「三河内曳山祭パンフレット」与謝野町三河内区曳山連合会、どでさっさ共和国、2018年 * 京都新聞社『ふるさとNEXT 京都府北部地域で生きる』京都新聞出版センター、2018年 == Related Articles == {{Commonscat|Shidori-jinja (Yosano, Kyoto)}} * {{ill|List of Shinto shrines in Kyoto Prefecture|en}} {{citation needed|Shidori '''Shidori Shrine''' (少初位) {{Shrine |Name = '''Shidori Shrine''' (倭文神社) |image = [[File:Sidori Shrine in yosano-cho.jpg|270px]]
{{ill|approach|de|Zugang|ja|参道|zh|參道}} |Location = {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|de|Präfektur Kyōto|ja|京都府|zh|京都府}}{{ill|Yosa District|de|Yosa-gun|ja|与謝郡|zh|与謝郡}}{{ill|Yosano|de|Yosano (Gemeinde)|ja|与謝野町|zh|与謝野町}} Mikochi 1453 |Position = {{Coord|format=dms|region:JP-26_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} |Enshrined deity = {{ill|Amano-hatsuchio no Kami|de|Amano-hatsuchio no Kami|ja|天羽槌雄神|1=Takehazuchi|2=ja|3=天羽槌雄神|4=zh|5=天羽槌雄神|6=fr|7=Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi|zh|天羽槌雄神}} (also called {{ill|Shidori no Ōkami|de|Shidori no Ōkami|ja|倭文大神|zh|倭文大神}}) |Sacred object = |Shrine rank = {{ill|Former Village Shrine|de|ehemaliger Dorfschrein|ja|旧村社|zh|旧村社}}
{{ill|Prefectural Shrine|de|Präfekturheiligtum|ja|府社|zh|府社}} |Founded = {{ill|710|de|Jahr 710|ja|710年|zh|710年}} ({{ill|Wadō|de|Wadō-Zeit|ja|和銅|zh|和銅}} 3) originally on Mount Ishizaki; moved here in {{ill|1653|de|Jahr 1653|ja|1653年|zh|1653年}} ({{ill|Teiō|de|Teiō-Zeit|ja|貞応|zh|貞応}} 2). |Chief priest = |Main hall = Irimoya-zukuri. In {{ill|1996|de|Jahr 1996|ja|1996年|zh|1996年}} ({{ill|Heisei|de|Heisei-Zeit|ja|平成|zh|平成}} 8) designated as a Kyoto Prefectural Cultural Property. |Alternative name = Ishizaki Shidori Daimyōjin |Fuda places etc.= |Annual festival= May 4 – Mikochi Hikiyama Festival (registered as Kyoto Prefecture Intangible Folk Cultural Property) |Shinto rituals = May 2 – Shinkōsai
May 3 – Yoimiya
May 4 – Kankōsai |Map = {{Location map|Japan Kyoto|label={{ill|Shidori Shrine|de|Shidori-Schrein|ja|倭文神社|zh|倭文神社}}|position=bottom|width=200|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=15|float=center|caption=}} {{Infobox mapframe|zoom=12|marker=religious-shinto|frame-width=200}} }} '''Shidori Shrine''' (倭文神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|de|Shintō-Schrein|ja|神社|zh|神社}} in the Mikochi (みごち) district of {{ill|Yosano|de|Yosano (Gemeinde)|ja|与謝野町|zh|与謝野町}}, {{ill|Yosa District|de|Yosa-gun|ja|与謝郡|zh|与謝郡}}, {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|de|Präfektur Kyōto|ja|京都府|zh|京都府}}. It is a historic shrine recorded as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|de|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社|zh|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|de|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|ja|延喜式神名帳|zh|延喜式神名帳}} compiled in {{ill|927|de|Jahr 927|ja|927年|zh|927年}} ({{ill|Enchō (Japan)|de|Enchō (Ära)|ja|延長 (日本)|zh|延長 (日本)|lt=延長}} 5).『野田川町誌』野田川町、1969年、570頁。 There are fourteen shrines called “Shidori Shrine” (倭文神社) across Japan that appear in the Engishiki, two of which lie in the Tango region of northern Kyoto Prefecture. This article concerns the one recorded as “Shidori Shrine, Tango Province, Yosa District.”「たんご通信5号」丹後リゾート推進連絡協議会、丹後リゾート総合企画株式会社、1996年、10頁。 Both the shrine itself and its annual festival, the Mikochi Hikiyama Festival, were recognized in April {{ill|2017|de|Jahr 2017|ja|2017年|zh|2017年}} ({{ill|Heisei|de|Heisei-Zeit|ja|平成|zh|平成}} 29) by the {{ill|Agency for Cultural Affairs|de|Kulturbehörde (Japan)|ja|文化庁|zh|文化庁}} as part of the “{{ill|Tango Chirimen Corridor|de|Seidenstraße von Tango|ja|丹後ちりめん回廊|zh|丹後ちりめん回廊}},” a Japanese Heritage story that conveys the region’s historical and cultural appeal.{{Cite web|和書|author=文化庁|authorlink=文化庁|date=|url=https://www.bunka.go.jp/seisaku/bunkazai/nihon_isan/pdf/nihon_isan_pamphlet_2019.pdf|title=日本遺産認定ストーリー一覧|work=「日本遺産（Japan Heritage）」について|accessdate=2020-11-11}}{{Cite web|和書|author=文化庁|authorlink=文化庁|date=|url=https://japan-heritage.bunka.go.jp/ja/stories/story043/index.html|title=300年を紡ぐ絹が織り成す丹後ちりめん回廊|website=日本遺産ポータルサイト|accessdate=2020-11-11}} == History == [[File:倭文神社（京都府与謝野町）.jpg|thumb|Shidori Shrine (Yosa), front view]] According to various records, the shrine was founded in {{ill|710|de|Jahr 710|ja|710年|zh|710年}} ({{ill|Wadō|de|Wadō-Zeit|ja|和銅|zh|和銅}} 3) or {{ill|712|de|Jahr 712|ja|712年|zh|712年}} (Wadō 5), when the deity Shidori no Ōkami was enshrined on Ishizaki Mountain in the village of Osa. At that time, Imperial orders to weave high-quality textiles (called “ayanishiki”A term for fine silk fabric.) were carried out in the area, and it is said that Laughing Oshi from the {{ill|Amabe clan|de|Amabe-Clan|ja|海部氏|zh|海部氏}} at {{ill|Kono Shrine|de|Kono-Schrein|ja|籠神社|zh|籠神社}}, the Ichinomiya of {{ill|Tango Province|de|Tango (Provinz)|ja|丹後国|zh|丹後国}}, was granted an imperial command to enshrine the deity. Legend holds that {{ill|Emperor Daigo|de|Kaiser Daigo|ja|醍醐天皇|zh|醍醐天皇}} also worshiped here.From the explanatory board at the shrine office (社務所). In {{ill|981|de|Jahr 981|ja|981年|zh|981年}} ({{ill|Tenroku|de|Tenroku-Zeit|ja|天禄|zh|天禄}} 12) the shrine was raised to Second Rank, and in {{ill|1223|de|Jahr 1223|ja|1223年|zh|1223年}} ({{ill|Teiō|de|Teiō-Zeit|ja|貞応|zh|貞応}} 2) it was relocated to its current site.{{Cite web|和書|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181009064805/http://www.geocities.jp/engisiki/tango/bun/tag390213-01.html |title=丹後国式内社 |publisher=阜嵐健|accessdate=2018-07-08}} Shrine tradition states that “in ancient times, people gathered under the sacred tree of the deity, offered treasures, made offerings, and rang treasure vessels to pray for a good harvest,” and a bronze bell was later unearthed in the precincts. Since ancient times, local residents of Mikochi have worshiped Shidori Shrine as their {{ill|Ubusuna-gami|de|Ubusuna-Gott|ja|産土神|zh|产土神}}.江原護『古代への旅 丹後』アジェンダ・プロジェクト、2004年、127頁。 Weaving remains a key local industry, best known through {{ill|Tango chirimen|de|Tango-Chirimen|ja|丹後ちりめん|zh|丹後ちりめん}}, and on festival days people from nearby villages traditionally came en masse carrying bundles of hemp fiber.『京都の社寺建築 与謝・丹後編』京都府埋蔵文化財保護基金、1984年、132頁。 An ink inscription from {{ill|1808|de|Jahr 1808|ja|1808年|zh|1808年}} ({{ill|Culture (era)|de|Ära Bunka|ja|文化|1=Bunka|2=ja|3=文化 (元号)|4=de|5=Bunka (Ära)|6=ko|7=분카|zh|文化}} 5) was discovered on the shrine’s roof during repairs. In earlier periods, under {{ill|Shinbutsu-shūgō|de|Shinbutsu-shūgō|ja|神仏習合|zh|神仏習合}}, the shrine was variously known as “Ishizaki Daimyōjin” or “Ishizaki Shidori Daimyōjin.” However, after the early Meiji {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|de|Shinbutsu-bunri|ja|神仏分離令|zh|神仏分離令}} policy separated Shinto and Buddhism, it was officially renamed “Shidori Shrine.” In {{ill|1907|de|Jahr 1907|ja|1907年|zh|1907年}} (Meiji 40), the shrine was designated for {{ill|heihakusai|en}} (imperial offerings). In {{ill|1873|de|Jahr 1873|ja|1873年|zh|1873年}} (Meiji 6) it was ranked as a Village Shrine, and in {{ill|1944|de|Jahr 1944|ja|1944年|zh|1944年}} (Showa 19), on November 20, it was elevated to Prefectural Shrine.神祗院第19第33號 At that time, there were originally two annual festivals—on April 25 and on May 1 when imperial offerings were presented—but nowadays only the spring festival in early May remains.『野田川町誌』野田川町、1969年、411頁。 In {{ill|2017|de|Jahr 2017|ja|2017年|zh|2017年}} (Heisei 29), the shrine and its spring festival, the Mikochi Hikiyama Festival, were officially recognized as part of the Japan Heritage “Tango Chirimen Corridor.”{{Cite web|和書|author=文化庁|authorlink=|date=|url=https://www.bunka.go.jp/seisaku/bunkazai/nihon_isan/|title=「日本遺産（Japan Heritage）」について|work=|language=日本語|accessdate=2018-2-20}}{{Cite web|和書|author=文化庁|authorlink=|date=|url=https://japan-heritage.bunka.go.jp/ja/stories/story043/index.html|title=日本遺産ポータルサイト「丹後ちりめん回廊」|work=|language=日本語|accessdate=2018-2-20}} == Enshrined Deities and Subsidiary Shrines == The main enshrined deity is {{ill|Amano-hatsuchio no Kami|de|Amano-hatsuchio no Kami|ja|天羽槌雄神|1=Takehazuchi|2=ja|3=天羽槌雄神|4=zh|5=天羽槌雄神|6=fr|7=Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi|zh|天羽槌雄神}}, also known as {{ill|Takehazuchi no Mikoto|de|Takehazuchi no Mikoto|ja|建葉槌命|zh|建葉槌命}}. Descendants of the ancient {{ill|Shidori clan|en}} revere him as Shidori no Ōkami. According to mythology, when {{ill|Amaterasu|de|Amaterasu|ja|天照大神|zh|天照大神}} hid in the Heavenly Rock Cave, this god was commanded by {{ill|Takamimusubi|de|Takamimusubi|ja|高皇産霊神|zh|高皇産霊神}} to weave cloth, thus becoming the ancestral deity of weaving. He is also regarded as a god of martial valor, often worshipped together with the war deity {{ill|Hachiman|de|Hachiman|ja|八幡神|zh|八幡神}}.「三河内曳山祭パンフレット」与謝野町三河内区曳山連合会、どでさっさ共和国、2018年 As for subsidiary shrines within the grounds, facing from the large torii on the prefectural road, there is an {{ill|Awashima Shrine|de|Awashima-Schrein|ja|粟嶋神社|zh|粟嶋神社}} on the right, an {{ill|Inari Shrine|de|Inari-Schrein|ja|稲荷神社|zh|稻荷神社}} partway toward the haiden on the right, and a Wakamiya Shrine (若宮社) on the left. File:倭文神社(与謝) 粟嶋社（鳥居右）.jpg|Awashima Shrine File:倭文神社(与謝) 稲荷社（向かって右）.jpg|Inari Shrine File:倭文神社(与謝) 若宮社 (向かって左).jpg|Wakamiya Shrine == Precinct and Cultural Properties == === Buildings === In addition to the main hall, dance stage, and worship hall which stand in a row, the precinct includes a storehouse, shrine gate, administrative office, and so on. The main hall was rebuilt after a fire in the Ka’ei era. According to the shrine’s “Rekidaiki” record, the current structure dates from {{ill|1821|de|Jahr 1821|ja|1821年|zh|1821年}} ({{ill|Bunsei|de|Bunsei-Zeit|ja|文政|zh|文政}} 4). It is an {{ill|irimoya-zukuri|en}} with copper roofing, a typical one-bay design. A karahafu-gabled {{ill|kouhai (architecture)|en|向拝}} extends from the front. The hall has balconies on three sides, with a protruding platform and steps in front. There are carved wooden doors on the front (double-folding) and sides (two-panel), and the interior divides into an inner sanctum and an even deeper sanctuary. The hall’s pillars are secured by beams and clamps, and a notable feature is its complex bracket structure (two-step brackets with additional bracket arms supporting round rafters, plus decorative patterns). The coffered ceiling of the kouhai is typical of Edo-period Tango shrines, also seen at the {{ill|Hiyoshi Shrine (Miyazu)|ja|日吉神社 (宮津市)|zh|日吉神社 (宮津市)}} main hall (built in {{ill|1688|de|Jahr 1688|ja|1688年|zh|1688年}}) and the tutelary shrine at {{ill|Nariai-ji|de|Nariai-ji|ja|成相寺|zh|成相寺}} (built in {{ill|1676|de|Jahr 1676|ja|1676年|zh|1676年}}). The rich carvings on the side panels and doors, including motifs from the Chinese legend of Huang Shigong and Zhang Liang, lions, and peonies, show a resemblance to the famed Karamon gate of the {{ill|Nishi Hongan-ji|de|Nishi Hongan-ji|ja|西本願寺|zh|西本願寺}} in Kyoto. As an important example of late-Edo-era shrine architecture in Tango, it was designated a Kyoto Prefectural Cultural Property in {{ill|1996|de|Jahr 1996|ja|1996年|zh|1996年}} (Heisei 8).{{Cite web|和書|url=http://www.kyoto-be.ne.jp/bunkazai/cms/?page_id=271 |title=京都府指定文化財一覧|publisher=京都府教育庁指導部文化財保護課|accessdate=2018-07-08}} The shinmon (main gate) has a gabled roof with pantiles, is three bays wide, one bay deep, and stands on eight pillars. The haiden (worship hall) is irimoya-zukuri with pantiles, six bays along the front, and a one-bay extension in front. File:倭文神社(与謝).jpg|Midway torii. Inari Shrine (right), Wakamiya Shrine (left). File:倭文神社(与謝) 神門.jpg|Shinmon File:倭文神社（京都府与謝野町）3.jpg|Haiden File:倭文神社(与謝) 拝殿.jpg|Haiden, with the dance stage and main hall behind it. File:倭文神社（京都府与謝野町）4.jpg|View from the dance stage to the main hall File:倭文神社（京都府与謝野町）5.jpg|The main hall File:倭文神社（京都府与謝野町）6.jpg|Main hall exterior File:倭文神社(与謝)本殿（江戸時代後期）.jpg|Main hall ceiling area (front) File:倭文神社(与謝)本殿（江戸時代後期）左側面.jpg|Carvings (left side panel) File:倭文神社(与謝)本殿（江戸時代後期）左.jpg|Ceiling area (left side) File:倭文神社(与謝)本殿（江戸時代後期）右側面.jpg|Carvings (right side panel) File:倭文神社(与謝)本殿（江戸時代後期）右.jpg|Ceiling area (right side) File:倭文神社（京都府与謝野町）7.jpg|Exterior of haiden, dance stage, and main hall === Historic Sites === Within the shrine precincts lie four ancient tumuli known as the Ishizaki Tombs or Shidori Shrine Kofun Group: Mound #1 (circular, 4 m high, 15 m diameter), #2 (circular, 2.5 m high, 10 m diameter), #3 (circular, 2 m high, 7 m diameter), and one keyhole-shaped tumulus about 60 m in total length. Their direct relationship to the shrine is not clearly established, but they are presumed to date to the mid-Kofun period (5th century). A Preservation Society was formed in {{ill|1930|de|Jahr 1930|ja|1930年|zh|1930年}} (Showa 5). From the tumuli, there is a panoramic view of Mikochi district and Mount Ōe. The entire shrine area is protected as part of the “Shidori Shrine Cultural Properties Preservation District” by Kyoto Prefecture.{{Cite web|和書|url=http://www.pref.kyoto.jp/kankyo/rdb/eco/sd/sd027.html |title=文化財環境保全地区 |publisher=京都府|accessdate=2018-07-08}} File:倭文神社（京都府与謝野町）２.jpg|Precinct view File:倭文神社(与謝) 古墳群.jpg|Four ancient tombs on the left side of the grounds File:倭文神社(与謝)古墳群上から.jpg|Looking down toward the shrine from the tombs File:倭文神社(与謝)古墳群からの眺望.jpg|Panorama from the tumuli == External Subsidiary Shrines == In addition to the main precinct, the shrine maintains outer shrines scattered around the town: Takamine-sha on Okadayama, Ozaki Kojinsha in Umedani, Atago-sha in Okuyama, Ebisu-sha in Daidō, Itsukushima-sha in Moriya, Shibunashi-sha in Nakatsubo, and Osaoka-sha further in the interior.『野田川町誌』野田川町、1969年、571頁。 There is also an Inari-sha in Fukumori. == Parishioners and the Mikochi Hikiyama Festival == [[File:三河内曳山祭４.jpg|thumb|Mikochi Hikiyama Festival procession]] [[File:三河内曳山祭2.jpg|thumb|The procession enters Miyamae Street]] [[File:倭文神社(与謝)参道.jpg|thumb|Miyamae Street]] This annual festival is said to have started in {{ill|1755|de|Jahr 1755|ja|1755年|zh|1755年}} ({{ill|Hōreki|de|Hōreki-Zeit|ja|宝暦|zh|宝暦}} 5) and flourished with the growth of the local textile industry, {{ill|Tango chirimen|de|Tango-Chirimen|ja|丹後ちりめん|zh|丹後ちりめん}}. It was once called the Hassaku Festival, held on the first day of the eighth month of the lunar calendar, but around {{ill|1887|de|Jahr 1887|ja|1887年|zh|1887年}} (Meiji 20) it became part of the {{ill|Kayadani Festival|en}} for the nearby {{ill|Tenman Shrine (Kayacho)|en|天満神社 (加悦)|ja|天満神社 (京都府与謝野町)|zh|天満神社 (京都府与謝野町)}} and took place every April 24–25. In {{ill|1991|de|Jahr 1991|ja|1991年|zh|1991年}} (Heisei 3), it separated from the Kayadani Festival and was moved to May 3–4.Because weaving declined and more parishioners took jobs requiring weekday attendance, they could no longer assemble the heavy floats on weekdays.京都新聞社『ふるさとNEXT 京都府北部地域で生きる』京都新聞出版センター、2018年、164-165頁。 This event, officially called the “Mikochi Hikiyama Gyōji,” is designated a Kyoto Prefecture {{ill|Intangible Folk Cultural Property|de|immaterielles Volkskulturgut|ja|無形民俗文化財|zh|无形民俗文化财}}.{{Cite web|和書|url=http://www.kyoto-kankou.or.jp/info_search/?event_id=7548&r=1531059533.3514 |title=三河内曳山祭 |publisher=|accessdate=2018-07-08}} '''The Mikochi Hikiyama Festival''' begins May 2 with the Shinkōsai, continues May 3 with a vigil (Yoimiya), and culminates on May 4 with the main festival day including sacred dances, the “calling of the gods” (kamiobiki), float processions, and the Kankōsai that returns the deities to their seats. === Float Procession (Hikiyama) === A giant banner leads the parade, followed by Kaguraden, large mountain floats, smaller children’s floats, and so on—about twelve floats in total. The largest are the yama (mountain) floats and the gei (performance) floats, which alternate participation every other year. In {{ill|2018|de|Jahr 2018|ja|2018年|zh|2018年}} (Heisei 30), the yama floats made the rounds. Parishioners from six sub-districts of Mikochi gather at their boundary lines with matching happi coats, bringing their floats. The giant banner from Umeya leads, followed by shrine officials, men carrying halberds and umbrellas, then each district’s floats.『野田川町誌』野田川町、1969年、412-413頁。 From the community center, one can see the line of floats in a long procession. Each yama float has its own musical accompaniment, while the children’s taiko float beats a large drum. Upon reaching the great torii and entering Miyamae Street, all converge on the same rhythm, called Tenjin-bayashi, with shouts of “dodesassa, dodesassa” and the pounding drum “dodendon-don, dodendon-don.”江原護『古代への旅 丹後』アジェンダ・プロジェクト、2004年、128頁。 During the procession, the “kamiobiki” (god-invitation) rite takes place, and once arrived at Shidori Shrine, ceremonial dances are offered. In the past, the kagura dancers would also make rounds to purify each home’s hearth, but now that survives only in an abbreviated form at the eve of the festival (May 3) in front of the shrine and each float, as well as in brief offerings on the morning of May 4. Below is a general table of the main floats and their characteristics. {| class="wikitable" |+Key floats of the Mikochi Hikiyama Festival !Parish (District)!!Float Name!!Enshrined Kami!!Crest!!Happi Coat!!Music/Chant Variety!!Float Notes |- |Umeya (Ōnobori) |Ōnobori Banner |{{ill|Amano-hatsuchio no Kami|de|Amano-hatsuchio no Kami|ja|天羽槌雄神|1=Takehazuchi|2=ja|3=天羽槌雄神|4=zh|5=天羽槌雄神|6=fr|7=Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi|zh|天羽槌雄神}} |Maru-ni-mitsu-aoi (triple hollyhock) |Crest on back; “Ōnobori” on collar; eight plum blossoms at hem |N/A |~6m high, 1.6m wide, 3.3m deep |- |Nakagumi |Hachiman-yama |{{ill|Emperor Ōjin|de|Kaiser Ōjin|ja|応神天皇|zh|应神天皇}} (Honada Wake no Mikoto) |Clustered arrows |Doves throughout the design |Various chants: “Yāma yāma,” “Kōrya kōrya,” “Tentetsu-shan-shan,” “Hotei-bayashi,” “Ichichiri hyu-hyuttose,” “Hanagasa-ondo,” “Oppiki taitaino-e,” “Beppin naika,” “O-mawari,” “hayashi-komi,” etc. |Height ~4.6m, width ~2.95m, depth ~3.62m |- |Shidori-chō |Shidori-yama |Shidori no Ōkami |Maru-ni-mitsu-aoi |Hollyhock leaves plus an itoguruma (thread-spinning wheel), symbol of weaving |Various: “Hayashi-komi,” “Yāma yāma,” “Kōrya kōrya,” “Doshitai doshitai,” “Ikkyō āiya,” “Manda,” “Tenjin-bayashi,” “Hādondon,” “Ākorya-korya,” “Beppin naika,” “Kompira fune fune,” “Hitotsutosei,” “Oppiki taitai,” etc. |Height ~4.7m, width ~3m, depth ~3.65m |- |Omotemachi |Kasuga-yama |{{ill|Takemikazuchi|de|Takemikazuchi|ja|武甕槌神|zh|武甕槌神}} (Kashima no Ōkami) |Descending wisteria |Falling maple leaves and flowing water pattern |Tenjin-bayashi, Ikken-sho, Juuni-kagura, Koma, Hotei-bayashi, Take-bayashi, Mawari, “Kompira fune fune,” “Oppiki taitai,” “Kazuu-ta,” etc. (many) |Began with a carried float in {{ill|Culture 3|en}}, turned into a yama float in Meiji 25. Height ~4.5m, width 3m, depth 3.7m. Formerly limited to male performers, but from {{ill|2016|de|Jahr 2016|ja|2016年|zh|2016年}} (Heisei 28) females also participate on the float. |- |Kaminomachi |Urashima-yama |{{ill|Kagutsuchi|de|Kagutsuchi|ja|カグツチ|zh|迦具土}} (Atago deity) and {{ill|Ukemochi no Kami|en}} (Inari deity) |Single turtle in a circle |Crest of waves |Many: Tenjin-bayashi, Ikken-sho, Koma, Juuni-kagura, Sasa-bayashi, Hotei-bayashi, “Take ni suzume,” “Yuka-shita,” “O-mawari,” etc. |Formed in Meiji 25 when the towns worshipping Atago and Inari merged. Height ~4.87m, width 3.31m, depth 4.24m. |- |Kagura-chō |Kagura-den |Shishi-gashira (lion’s head) |Mitsu-domoe |Three commas plus peonies |Gion-bayashi. Dances include hei-no-mai, ken-no-mai, shihō-kake, midare-no-mai, etc. |~3.65m tall, 2.27m wide, 3.15m deep |} === Kamiobiki (“Calling the Gods”) === Also called “kamiobi” in local speech. According to oral tradition, the shrine’s main deity, {{ill|Amano-hatsuchio no Kami|de|Amano-hatsuchio no Kami|ja|天羽槌雄神|1=Takehazuchi|2=ja|3=天羽槌雄神|4=zh|5=天羽槌雄神|6=fr|7=Takehazuchi|lt=Takehazuchi|zh|天羽槌雄神}}, was once married to {{ill|Suseri-hime|de|Suseri-Hime|ja|須勢理媛|zh|須勢理媛}}, enshrined at {{ill|Sushiro Shrine|en|須代神社|ja|須代神社|zh|須代神社}} in the nearby Akashi district across the river. However, because Suseri-hime became the principal wife of the mighty {{ill|Ōkuninushi|de|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主命|zh|大国主命}}, the two were forced to part ways, and they can reunite only during this annual festival. During the float procession, at the Sugikoshi Bridge over the Okuyama River, participants pour sacred sake and rice into the river three times. A representative from Umeya holds up a gohei and calls eastward with three loud “Ō~i!” In local lore, Suseri-hime rests beneath the “pine tree on the riverbank” at the halfway point of the {{ill|Nodagawa (Kyoto)|de|Nodagawa (Fluss)|ja|野田川 (京都府)|zh|野田川}}, hears the call, and joins the procession so she and her husband can be together again for the festival. It is also said that her brothers, {{ill|Kuraokami no Kami|en}} (the deity of rice) and {{ill|Mikumari|fr|Mikumari|ja|水分神|lt=Ame no mikumari no Kami}} (the deity of offering), join in at the same call, thus forming a group of deities who jointly conduct the festival. == Access == ;Address * 1453 Mikochi, {{ill|Yosano|de|Yosano (Gemeinde)|ja|与謝野町|zh|与謝野町}}, {{ill|Yosa District|de|Yosa-gun|ja|与謝郡|zh|与謝郡}}, {{ill|Kyoto Prefecture|de|Präfektur Kyōto|ja|京都府|zh|京都府}} ;Transportation * From {{ill|Yosano Station|en|与謝野駅|ja|与謝野駅|zh|与謝野駅}} on the {{ill|Kyoto Tango Railway|de|Kyoto Tango Bahn|ja|京都丹後鉄道|zh|京都丹後鉄道}}, take a bus by {{ill|Kaya Kōsan|en}} and get off at “Mikochi-guchi.”江原護『古代への旅 丹後』アジェンダ・プロジェクト、2004年、129頁。 * Take the {{ill|Tankai Bus|en|丹海バス|ja|丹海バス|zh|丹海バス}} Yosa or Fukuchiyama lines to “Mikochi Elementary School Stop.” == Notes == == References == == Further Reading == * 江原護『古代への旅 丹後』アジェンダ・プロジェクト、2004年 * 『野田川町誌』野田川町、1969年 * 『京都の社寺建築 与謝・丹後編』京都府埋蔵文化財保護基金、1984年 * 「三河内曳山祭パンフレット」与謝野町三河内区曳山連合会、どでさっさ共和国、2018年 * 京都新聞社『ふるさとNEXT 京都府北部地域で生きる』京都新聞出版センター、2018年 == Related Articles == {{Commonscat|Shidori-jinja (Yosano, Kyoto)}} *
